articles.title: CONEXPO-CON/AGG 2026 recap

paras.en: CONEXPO-CON/AGG 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada, reaffirmed its position as the largest construction trade show in North America, drawing more than 140,000 construction professionals from 128 countries across the globe. For Carlisle Brake & Friction, a CentroMotion brand, the week was an incredible opportunity to showcase innovation, strengthen partnerships and gain valuable insights into the future of the construction, mining and aggregate industries. Throughout the busy week, attendees had the chance to speak with our experts and watch live demonstrations of our brake systems, along with our advanced brake and transmission friction solutions for the construction industry.

Top trends included integrating autonomous equipment, advanced digital tools and sustainable technologies. The exhibition footprint spanned more than 3 million square feet with greater than 2,000 exhibitors, and attendees covered miles of exhibits sprawled across indoor and outdoor spaces.

At the show, Carlisle Brake & Friction highlighted its advanced brake systems and friction technologies designed to withstand extreme duty cycles and demanding off‑highway applications. The CentroMotion booth was a hub of activity, and the team welcomed OEM leaders and aftermarket specialists. These interactions went beyond showcasing our products, they enhanced relationships and increased our team’s understanding of the industry’s evolving needs. articles.title: New Facility Brings Off-Highway Wet Friction Production to India

paras.en: New Facility Brings Off-Highway Wet Friction Production to India

Carlisle Brake & Friction has broken ground to expand its Chennai, India manufacturing operations in one of the world’s fastest-growing industrial regions. Having produced mechatronic products in the region for more than 15 years, Carlisle CBF will relocate to add production at a larger site for off-highway paper wet friction discs and steel separator plates. The new facility is scheduled to open in 2027.

The move to expanded space is designed to accommodate manufacturing capabilities needed to serve the growing demand across the agriculture, construction and especially mining industries in India and Southeast Asia. Local production will improve supply chain responsiveness while supporting original equipment and aftermarket requirements in cost-sensitive markets.

Carlisle Brake & Friction is establishing a state-of-the-art wet friction manufacturing facility on par with proven global manufacturing processes in the new Chennai plant, to build a more resilient regional platform. This expansion strengthens our ability to deliver durable wet friction products that help keep critical off-highway equipment productive.

articles.title: Why Freshly Refinished Paint Requires a Different Approach to Detailing
articles.author: Justin Glass

paras.en: A vehicle can leave a collision repair facility looking excellent under shop lighting and still present a completely different set of challenges when it reaches a detailer weeks or months later. From a detailing perspective, one of the most important things to understand is that refinished paint should not automatically be treated the same way as an untouched factory finish.

During more than 20 years of professional detailing, and as owner of Fort Lauderdale Precise Mobile Auto Detailing, I’ve worked on vehicles with original paint, repainted panels and combinations of both. Those jobs have taught me that the first step should never be reaching for a polisher. It should be determining what you’re actually working on.

Factory paint already varies considerably from manufacturer to manufacturer. Once collision repair and refinishing enter the picture, the variables increase. Film build, curing history, sanding and polishing performed during the repair, previous corrections and the condition of adjacent factory panels can all influence how the finish should be approached.

For a detailer, the goal is not simply to make the paint look as perfect as possible. The goal is to improve the appearance while preserving enough material for the finish to remain healthy over the long term.

When I inspect a vehicle that has had body or paint work, I want to know which panels have been refinished before I make decisions about correction. Sometimes the difference is obvious. Other times, a quality refinish blends so well that visual inspection alone does not tell the whole story.

That is where careful inspection, good lighting and paint-thickness measurements become useful. A paint-thickness gauge cannot tell a detailer everything about a finish, and readings must be interpreted correctly, but comparing panels can reveal significant differences in film build. It can also help identify areas where previous sanding or polishing may have occurred.

The important point is that a detailer should not assume every panel has the same amount of material available to work with. A hood may still have its factory finish while a fender and door have been refinished. Treating all three panels identically simply because they’re on the same vehicle can be a mistake.

Refinished paint does not always respond to polishing the way surrounding factory paint does. Depending on the paint system, application, cure, prior finishing work and environmental conditions, a refinished panel may cut or finish differently from an adjacent original panel.

A combination that works beautifully on one panel may be unnecessarily aggressive on another — which is why test spots matter. I would rather begin conservatively and increase correction only when the finish tells me it’s necessary than start aggressively and discover afterward that I removed more material than the job required.

Detailers also need to respect the refinisher’s recommendations regarding cure time and post-refinish care. Paint systems and repair procedures differ, so a blanket rule about when a newly painted vehicle can be polished, sealed, coated or otherwise treated is not a substitute for information about the specific repair. When there is uncertainty, communication with the collision facility or paint manufacturer is the safer approach.
Do Not Correct a Panel Twice Without Thinking

One issue that’s easy to overlook is that a refinished panel may already have undergone substantial finishing before the customer ever sees it. Depending on the repair, the surface may have been denibbed, sanded, compounded and polished to remove texture or defects.

If a detailer later sees a few remaining imperfections and immediately performs another aggressive correction, the panel can effectively be corrected twice. The customer may see a small visual improvement, but additional clearcoat has been removed to achieve it.

That trade-off matters. Clearcoat is not an unlimited resource. Every sanding or polishing step that removes measurable material reduces what remains for future correction. A vehicle may need to survive years of washing, environmental exposure and additional cosmetic work. Preserving the finish should therefore be part of the decision, not an afterthought.
Perfection Is Not Always the Safest Goal
Customers understandably want repaired areas to look perfect. Detailers want that too. But there are situations where chasing the final isolated defect is not the best decision for the vehicle.

If removing one deeper mark requires disproportionately aggressive sanding or polishing, I explain the trade-off. A defect that’s barely visible under normal conditions may be preferable to unnecessarily reducing the protective clearcoat around it. The same principle applies to factory paint, but it becomes particularly important when the history of a refinished panel isn’t completely known.

Professional correction requires judgment. The best result isn’t always the panel with the fewest visible defects under an inspection light. Sometimes the best result is the one that looks dramatically better while retaining as much of the finish as reasonably possible.
Edges, Body Lines and Blended Areas Need Respect

Edges and pronounced body lines deserve additional caution because paint film can be less forgiving in those areas, and polishing pressure and pad contact are harder to control. The same is true around tight contours, adjacent trim and transitions between repaired and original areas.

A detailer also has to recognize that a repaired area may extend beyond the most obvious damaged panel. Blending can involve adjacent panels to achieve a consistent color match. Knowing the repair history helps prevent assumptions about where the refinished area begins and ends.

This is another reason communication between collision repairers and detailers can be valuable. A simple explanation of which panels were refinished, blended or heavily finished can give the person caring for the vehicle later information that’s difficult to obtain from appearance alone.
Finishing Quality Affects the Customer’s Perception

From the customer’s perspective, the paint is often the most visible part of the repair. They may not understand the structural procedures, measuring systems or refinishing process that went into restoring the vehicle, but they’ll notice haze, holograms, sanding marks, compound residue and unfinished edges.
Those details can influence how the customer perceives the entire repair. A technically excellent repair deserves an equally thoughtful final presentation.

Good lighting is critical during the finishing stage. Defects that disappear under one type of shop lighting can become obvious in direct sunlight. Checking the finish under multiple lighting conditions helps identify haze or machine marks before the vehicle is delivered.

Residue around emblems, trim, panel gaps and edges also matters. These may seem like small details compared with the repair itself, but they’re exactly the details an owner may notice when inspecting the vehicle up close.

When a repaired vehicle comes to me later, my job is not to redo the body shop’s work. It’s to evaluate the finish that exists at that moment and choose the least aggressive process capable of producing the desired improvement.

That usually begins with proper washing and decontamination, followed by inspection under controlled lighting. If correction is necessary, I perform a test section before deciding on the combination for the rest of the panel. I also compare the behavior of refinished areas with original paint rather than assuming one process will work everywhere.

If something doesn’t look right, I would rather stop and gather more information than force a result. That can mean asking the customer about the repair, recommending that the collision facility inspect an issue or simply deciding that a particular defect should remain rather than removing excessive material.

Collision repairers, detailers and vehicle owners all benefit when the history of a finish is communicated clearly. The more a detailer knows about what was painted, blended, sanded or polished, the better the decisions that can be made later.

Customers also benefit from realistic aftercare instructions. They should understand that refinished paint needs appropriate care, that not every cosmetic imperfection should automatically be attacked aggressively and that future detailers should be told which areas have been repaired.

For detailers, asking a few questions before correction can prevent expensive mistakes. For collision shops, providing basic information about the refinishing work can help preserve the quality of the repair long after the vehicle leaves the facility.
Preservation Should Be Part of the Finish
The collision repair and detailing industries approach vehicles from different perspectives, but they share an important responsibility: protecting the work that has already been done.

A refinished panel should not be treated as simply another surface to compound until every visible defect disappears. Its history matters. Its remaining film build matters. The finishing work already performed matters. And the customer’s expectation for how the vehicle will look years from now matters, too.
After more than two decades of detailing, I’ve learned that restraint can be just as important as correction. Knowing how to polish paint is a skill. Knowing when to stop polishing is another one.

When freshly refinished paint is approached with proper evaluation, conservative testing and long-term preservation in mind, the result can look excellent without sacrificing more of the finish than necessary. That’s better for the detailer, better for the repairer and, most importantly, better for the vehicle owner.

articles.title: Fix Auto Inglewood Opens State-of-the-Art Collision Repair Facility in California
articles.author: Jason Stahl

paras.en: Fix Auto USA has announced the opening of Fix Auto Inglewood, located at 737 North La Brea Avenue in Inglewood, Calif.

Owned and operated by Nevin Baratian, Fix Auto Inglewood is a brand-new, fully equipped collision repair facility spanning more than 100,000 square feet. Built with the latest technology and state-of-the-art equipment, the facility is designed to provide comprehensive collision and mechanical repair services while delivering an exceptional customer experience.

Fix Auto Inglewood holds numerous OEM certifications, including: Alfa Romeo; Chrysler; Dodge; Jeep; Fiat; Ford; Hyundai; Kia; Genesis; General Motors; Honda ProFirst; Mazda; Nissan; Infiniti; and VinFast. BMW and Mercedes-Benz certifications are expected upon completion of ongoing training programs. Additionally, every member of the repair team is I-CAR Platinum.

“We are excited to introduce Fix Auto Inglewood to the community,” said Nevin Baratian, owner of Fix Auto Inglewood. “Our vision is to deliver exceptional collision repair services backed by industry-leading certifications, advanced technology and a highly trained team. As a family-owned business, we are committed to earning the trust of every customer while building strong relationships within the Inglewood community and supporting local charities and initiatives.”

Founded on the values of a family-owned collision repair business, Fix Auto Inglewood is dedicated to providing quality repairs, outstanding customer service, and meaningful support for local organizations and community initiatives.

“Fix Auto Inglewood represents the caliber of ownership and operational excellence that strengthens our network,” said Damien Reyna, Chief Operating Officer, Driven Brands Collision Group. “Nevin and his team have invested in a state-of-the-art facility, cutting-edge equipment, and advanced training to ensure customers receive safe, high-quality repairs. We are proud to welcome Fix Auto Inglewood to the Fix Auto USA family and look forward to supporting their continued growth and success.”
Please join the network in welcoming Fix Auto Inglewood to the Fix Auto USA family.
For more information visit FixAutoUSA.com.

articles.title: Audi plans to build first U.S. plant in Georgia
articles.author: Lurah Lowery

paras.en: Audi plans to build its first U.S. plant in Georgia at the Middle Georgia Mega Site. Construction is slated to begin in 2027.

A press release announcing the new project doesn’t include square footage, but it notes the $4 billion plant will be one of the brand’s largest production footprints globally. Annual assembly capacity will be 200,000 vehicles. Production is planned to begin in the early 2030s, “focused on Audi’s premium SUVs tailored to North American customers and designed to unlock significant growth potential in one of the world’s most important premium markets.”
The release adds that “the investment marks a long-term commitment to the United States and will establish North America as a major pillar of Audi’s global production network.”

“This project is a key element of a broader growth strategy focused on customer needs, a compelling product portfolio, and a more competitive business model,” the release states. “The investment is part of a long-term strategy for profitable growth.”
Gernot Döllner, Audi AG Board of Management chairman, states in the release that the goal is “building a stronger Audi business in America — not simply about building a factory.”

“We have much greater ambitions for Audi in America,” he said. “The United States is one of the world’s most important premium markets, and we have not yet realized our full potential. We are determined to change that — with premium products, a stronger brand, and a competitive local production base.”
Audi says Georgia provides an investment-ready site, a skilled workforce, an established automotive supplier network, and strong logistics infrastructure.
Audi hints at future U.S. investments in the release “as the brand continues to deepen its commitment to the American market.”

“Audi is building its future in America,” said Vito Paladino, Audi of America president, in the release. “As part of our larger U.S. strategy, we are focused on becoming an even more significant player in this market. This investment signifies the brand’s commitment to our customers, dealers, employees, and communities across the country.”

articles.title: How Cam Designs Are Meeting More Specialized Demands
articles.author: Greg Jones

paras.en: Picking a camshaft used to involve a simple flip through a catalog to find a grind that matched your basic engine specs. Today, off-the-shelf cams still make sense for many applications, but more specialized engine combinations are pushing builders toward more custom solutions. Experts attribute this shift to a handful of factors.

Nick Norris of Callies says the move away from “one-size-fits-most” cams is largely due to combinations becoming too specialized. The same basic engine, he notes, can be naturally aspirated, turbocharged, positive-displacement supercharged, or run with nitrous, and each can require a very different approach to valve timing.

“Better EFI, data acquisition and simulation have also changed what we can evaluate,” Norris says. “We can look at boost, backpressure, converter behavior, engine acceleration, and other data and design around what the vehicle actually needs. Instead of asking only what cam will make the most power, we can ask where we need the torque and how we want that power delivered.”

All of this has changed how Norris and other top manufacturers look at valvetrain development. While cam specs and events have traditionally been referenced to what’s happening at the lobe, “for the past couple of years I’ve been retraining myself to think more about the events at the valve,” he says. “After all, that’s what the engine sees.”

That shift – from designing around the camshaft itself to designing around what the valve actually does – is a big part of where cam development is headed. It also helps explain why manufacturers are moving beyond basic specs like lobe separation angle (LSA) and taking a more complete, system-level approach to the valvetrain.

Why exactly is the market evolving this way? One important driver, according to Bobby Biancaniello of Cam Motion, is “the ability to have a camshaft spec’d for your exact build and ground and shipped to you in one week’s time.”

While Cam Motion’s off-the-shelf grinds will work for almost any late-model application, he notes, when you start changing things like runner lengths on intakes, incorporating power adders, or adding displacement by lengthening the stroke, “it’s easier to make them exactly what they need with a custom grind than having a catalog with thousands of options” that can just end up complicating the selection process.

Another reason for this changing dynamic is the role of modern technology and tuning. Nic Woods of Clay Smith Cams explains that until about 10-15 years ago, EFI was a major headache for cam manufacturers, and “there were only a few guys in the country who really knew how to dial in performance cams and get them tuned and mapped correctly for the air-fuel ratio at idle.”
But now, with the rapid evolution of ECU technology and how well these systems communicate with the O2 sensors, today’s self-learning systems can better accommodate more aggressive performance cams.

“We don’t really have to recommend cams differently for fuel-injected platforms anymore,” Woods says. “We can give them the right cam, and if the guy doesn’t know how to tune it, the fuel injection can self-learn and map the fuel correctly.”

Charlie Westcott of Militia Racing Products points to manufacturing technology and material advances as additional factors influencing the market. He says many traditional cam cores are designed to cover a wide range of applications, which can create challenges when they’re machined and heat-treated.

By comparison, tool-steel cores (like S7) are high-strength throughout and can be manufactured more efficiently without some of the heat-treating and coating steps that materials like 8620 or 9310 would require.

“I can make a camshaft – from a phone call to the finished product – in about three days,” Westcott says. “Those three days are only because I’m waiting for the heat treat to come back. Whereas if you’re doing these other cams, you have to send them out to get copper-coated, then send them out again for heat treatment after you mill them. It’s a big time suck. I prefer getting things done quickly for people.”

Of course, to get a custom camshaft recommendation, certain information must be collected. Norris says the engine’s cubic inches, rpm range, cylinder heads, and application will get the Callies team in the ballpark. But choosing the actual profiles requires more detail.

“We’ll look at the weights of the valvetrain components and the overall stiffness of the system based on things like pushrod dimensions, rocker ratios and material, and the rest of the valvetrain configuration,” Norris says.
The spring package is another big consideration. If a customer has one they’re happy with, Norris and his team will go over the specs to make sure it’s compatible with the profiles they’ve chosen.

“If we’re starting from scratch, the spring and lobe need to be considered together rather than treating the spring as something that gets selected after the cam,” he notes. “Ultimately, the basic engine information helps determine the valve events and general cam specifications, while the details of the valvetrain help determine how aggressive the lobe profiles can be and still maintain control through the intended rpm range.”

Biancaniello agrees that when deciding on the best camshaft for a particular application, “it’s important for the cam guy to know as much as possible about the setup.” That means customers need to be as clear and up front as possible about their goals and how they plan to use the vehicle. Why? Because two builds that look virtually the same can require two very different cams.

As an example, he points to a turbocharged LS 5.3L with a set of 62mm turbos. In one case, the engine is being used in a streetcar with a tight converter, air conditioning, power brakes, and no transbrake. This customer wants very quick spool-up, a broad powerband, a 6,500-rpm ceiling, and 700-plus horsepower.

“That setup will have much different specs than the identical engine/turbos going into a drag race-only application with a transbrake and a converter that flashes 6,200-plus rpm and gets run to 8,000 rpm max on much higher boost levels with a goal of 1,200-plus hp,” he says.
Norris offers a similar assessment, making note of pressure conditions and the fact that the same boost level with two different turbo systems can produce very different exhaust backpressure.

“That affects how I approach exhaust timing and overlap,” Norris explains. “The engine specifications may look nearly identical on paper, but what the vehicle needs from the engine can lead to two very different camshafts.”

Woods, too, leaves no stone unturned when gathering information, wanting to know the compression, what cylinder head is being used, the flow numbers, the type of intake manifold, components in the bottom end, and more.

“We need to have some idea of whose brand piston is in there so we can get a good estimate of how much valve clearance we have and how much camshaft we can actually put in before he has a problem,” Woods says.

Once the specs are covered, it’s time to discuss the vehicle and its intended use, which gives manufacturers an idea of rpm range and where a customer wants power and torque to occur. “Some of these conversations can take five minutes; some can take two hours,” Woods admits. “At the end of the day, the cam is the same price, but a company has to be willing to put in that extra time to make sure the customer gets the exact right cam for his application.”

Westcott, whose customers include Pro Line Racing and Noonan Race Engineering, among others, sees plenty of unorthodox projects as well. His work has covered everything from a one-of-a-kind 1969 455-style Pontiac engine with a single overhead cam to a four-valve-per-cylinder, small block Oldsmobile W-30 (one of only two ever made) to an inline six-cylinder Holden race engine from Australia and a set of John Deere tractor pulling cams. At this point, it’s safe to say almost nothing is out of bounds.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Even so, Westcott still gets calls where he has to steer people away from potential trouble. One of the most common mistakes he encounters is customers focusing too heavily on aggressive lobe profiles to try to maximize area under the curve.

“I always say, you can’t make an engine good with the camshaft,” he states. “The camshaft, in my mind, is like the conductor of the orchestra. You’ve got your cylinder heads and your manifold, and your induction system is probably the most important thing. It really sets the rpm band for the engine. The camshaft has to match that stuff, so the camshaft comes last in the party.”

In other words, a cam can’t compensate for an engine combo that won’t support the desired rpm or power level. “You can’t take a stock small-block Chevy 350 and change the cam and think you’re going to make power at 10,000 rpm,” he adds. “That’s just not going to do it.”
Instead, he says, builders should focus on getting the entire combination right rather than trying to make up for shortcomings with an overly aggressive camshaft.

“I have to talk guys out of trying to make aggressive lobes because they think they need to square up the lobes to make the engine good,” Westcott says. “I tell them, you need to fix your heads and make the cam smooth. That way you’re not beating up parts.”

An overly aggressive cam can create unnecessary stress throughout the valvetrain. “If you have to get so aggressive that you’re beating up stuff, that’s never good,” he says. “If you’ve got a jackhammer for an engine, you want the engine to be nice and smooth and not have any problems. Work on the induction system.”

Another common mistake is simply going too large on duration. “You’re better off being 5 degrees short than 5 degrees big,” he says. “Everybody wants to have the cam be too big, but they’ll typically run better if they’re smaller than if they’re bigger.”

For Biancaniello, the biggest sticking point is unquestionably LSA. He says engine builders will often request a cam with a specific LSA and little else, expecting him to fill in the blanks. He has to remind them that LSA is only one part of the equation.

“Duration and centerlines are equally important pieces to that puzzle,” he says. “We need to choose the correct valve timing the setup wants,” adding that he encourages builders to reference Cam Motion’s cam timing calculator to better understand how changes in cam specs affect the engine’s behavior.

“I can make a camshaft ‘work’ with the LSA you might think is ideal for the setup,” Biancaniello says, “but the more ideal approach would have been picking the best open and close timing and letting the duration/LSA and centerlines fall wherever they fall to make those events timed where you want them.”

Norris tabs a common mistake as choosing a cam primarily from duration at .050” lift. While he notes that’s an important number, “it doesn’t tell you where the valve events occur or how the valve gets from the seat to peak lift and back.”

He also warns against concentrating too much on duration and lobe separation and overlooking the individual valve events. Intake closing, exhaust opening and the amount and location of overlap can have a major effect on where the engine makes torque and how it responds.

“The valvetrain also has to be considered,” Norris adds. “A lobe may look ideal from an airflow standpoint but be too aggressive for the lifter, rocker, valve, and spring combination. Making the cam more aggressive doesn’t help if the valvetrain becomes unstable before the engine reaches its intended rpm.”

As racing classes and enthusiast segments continue to become more specialized, application-specific camshaft development will undoubtedly progress in kind. Biancaniello expects the industry to head “down a further rabbit hole of constant testing, R&D and real-world data” to keep pace with the seemingly endless introduction of new segments and rulebooks on the competition side.

Norris sees the next step as combining traditional cam design with more detailed analysis of the complete valvetrain. Duration, lift and valve events will always be important, he says, “but we’re increasingly able to evaluate velocity, acceleration, jerk, radius of curvature and frequency content along with actual valve motion from Spintron testing.”

The long-term goal, then, is to put that data to work earlier in the cycle. “The ability to predict if and when the valvetrain will become unstable in software, verify it through Spintron testing and ultimately validate it on the dyno would take the development process to the next level,” Norris states.

Woods raises an interesting point about the future, and something he would like to see become more commonplace in the market: moving toward validated systems to prevent premature failures, especially in high-end builds.

“You get into those specialty racing applications and you test your lobe designs on a Spintron,” he says. “You have this rocker arm, this spring, this retainer, this pushrod, and this head, and then you sell the cam by itself – how does that make sense? It’s almost like you can only buy this cam with what we tested it with.

“That’s something I think the industry is really lacking: telling the customer that these lobes are specific for drag-racing applications, and you have to have this rocker, this spring, this retainer, and this diameter pushrod with this wall thickness. Otherwise, the results may vary. When it gets to those levels of application, you have to have the system. If one piece of that system isn’t in place, the likelihood of premature failure is evident. It’s impossible for it not to be.”

The bottom line is that off-the-shelf camshafts certainly have their place, but the direction of the industry is clear. As engine combinations get more specialized and manufacturers zero in on what’s happening at the valve, the cam is becoming less of an isolated component and increasingly one piece in a complete valvetrain system.

articles.title: How OE Tire Fitments Influence Replacement Tire Sales
articles.author: Denise Koeth

paras.en: An original equipment (OE) tire fitment can influence a customer’s next tire purchase years after a vehicle leaves the factory. Aaron Neumann, head of the Nexen Tire America Technical Center, estimates that around 30% of drivers request the same tire or brand when shopping for replacements. Among luxury vehicle owners, he says more than half choose the same brand.

For tire dealers, that familiarity creates an opportunity to turn OE tire fitments into replacement sales. But making the right recommendation requires understanding why automakers select particular tires, which customers want to preserve their vehicle’s original performance and when another tire might better meet their needs.
Neumann explains how OE partnerships influence consumer purchasing decisions and what dealers should consider when recommending replacement tires.

An OE tire can begin taking shape two to three years before its intended vehicle even reaches the market. Tiremakers earn an OE fitment on a vehicle through a multi-year, collaborative engineering and testing process with the auto manufacturer long before the vehicle goes into production.

“There is a high bar to earning OE fitment,” says Aaron Neumann, head of Nexen Tire America Technical Center. “Technically, a tire manufacturer has to prove they have a highly controlled production process with robust quality systems that pass very stringent audits. They also must have the technical capability to meet performance targets at the leading edge of tire technology, which is generally only within reach for Tier 1 and 2 manufacturers. Commercially, they need to show a top-level financial rating and logistically, need to show a 100% on-time global supply chain.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Neumann says many Hyundai, Kia, Ram and Jeep vehicles in the United States feature Nexen tires.

“Two fitments we’re particularly excited about right now are the Jeep Wrangler and the new Jeep Recon,” he says. “We are also very proud of our Porsche Panamera and Cayenne fitments. Those programs are good examples of the range of capabilities required in OE development. The performance targets for a Porsche are different from those of a Jeep, but in both cases the tire has to be engineered as part of the vehicle rather than treated as an off-the-shelf component.”
For a tire manufacturer, the rigorous process is worth it for both the added business and increased brand awareness.
While Nexen does see an increase in replacement sales for sizes with OE fitments, quantifying brand awareness is a little more difficult, according to Neumann.

“There are so many new brands in the market, and customers only need to think about tires once every few years, but OE creates familiarity over the entire ownership period,” he says. “Someone may see Nexen on their own vehicle, on a neighbor’s SUV or a spare OE Nexen Roadian HTX2 on the back of a Jeep Wrangler during their morning commute every day. They may not consciously think about it at the time, but that exposure helps make the brand familiar. That recognition matters when it becomes time to replace tires.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: That tendency to stick with an OE tire varies by vehicle segment and by what customers expect from their replacement tires.

“Understandably, luxury or performance owners are more sensitive to maintaining the way the vehicle was engineered to drive, so they place more value on staying with the OE brand or specification,” he says. “At the other end of the market, a value-oriented consumer may be more willing to compare brands based on price, mileage or another practical need.”
How OE Tire Fitments Influence Replacement Sales

When recommending replacement tires, ask customers what performance characteristics they want from their vehicles. Ask whether customers liked their OE tires and what driving conditions they regularly face. Then determine whether the OE fitment or another product is the best choice.

For luxury and performance vehicle owners, Neumann suggests considering which characteristics the driver wants to preserve, including steering response, ride quality, noise levels, braking and handling.

“Enthusiasts can be similar, although they may also be more willing to move away from the exact OE tire if they are deliberately trying to change a particular performance characteristic,” he adds. “That’s where understanding the customer’s priorities becomes important.

“Generally, OE specification carries more weight as vehicles become more specialized and customers become more sensitive to how the vehicle performs. That can include luxury cars, sports cars, performance SUVs and increasingly EVs, where factors such as rolling resistance, noise, vehicle weight and range can all make tire selection more noticeable.”

However, Neumann explains that in these instances, OE is not automatically the best replacement choice simply because of the vehicle type or price point. “The better question is whether the customer wants to preserve the original balance of performance or change it,” he notes.
From a customer’s point of view, it depends less on the vehicle and more on what they need from their tires.

“If they are happy with the OE tire’s performance, then replace them like for like,” Neumann says. “If they live in snow country, then they should upgrade to a tire marked with a three-peak mountain snowflake symbol. Now, if they do a lot of miles and would like better treadwear, then look for tires with longer treadwear warranties. If they have a truck and want to upgrade the appearance, look for a more aggressive A/T or R/T tire.”

He explains that when the switch is made from OE tires to a different product, there will be a trade-off, “perhaps 2 mpg of fuel economy or a little bit more tire noise,” but that many people think these trade-offs are worth making.
“I’m an advocate for teaching consumers about tire performance and trade-offs so they can make educated decisions when buying tires,” Neumann says.

articles.title: Magnaflow President Dan Paolone on the ‘Long-Term Play’
articles.author: Mary DellaValle

paras.en: This episode of DriveTime features Dan Paolone, president of Magnaflow.

Paolone said Magnaflow’s family-owned heritage has shaped both its culture and its long-term approach to the market. Founded in 1981 by his uncle, Jerry Paolone, the company has operated around a “build it and stand by it” philosophy while emphasizing lasting relationships and accountability from design through manufacturing. While Magnaflow is widely associated with performance exhaust, Paolone emphasized that the company is fundamentally an emissions and exhaust business, with approximately 10,000 SKUs across catalytic converters and BRExhaust. That breadth, combined with its premium performance brands, gives Magnaflow a much broader aftermarket presence than its performance reputation alone might suggest, he explained.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Vertical integration is another key part of Magnaflow’s strategy. Paolone said the company invests consistently in employees, infrastructure and capital to maintain greater control from research and development through manufacturing and distribution. That approach also extends to data, an area where Magnaflow has made significant investments. By controlling more of the process and supply chain, Paolone said the company gains flexibility while supporting its long-term strategy. That philosophy reflects Magnaflow’s broader approach to business: Rather than managing quarter to quarter, the company views each quarter as another step toward executing a plan measured in years and decades.

paras.en: Looking ahead, Paolone sees significant growth opportunities across Magnaflow’s existing emissions and exhaust business, BRExhaust and its expanding OE business. The company models vehicle trends through 2040 and expects hybrids, which still require catalytic converters and exhaust systems, to create additional opportunities. BRExhaust is also expanding by offering complete installation kits for repair shops that eliminate the need for welding, cutting or pipe bending, helping technicians complete more repairs in-house. On the OE side, Magnaflow sees an opportunity to serve lower-volume platforms, particularly vehicles in the 10,000- to 20,000-unit range, where its infrastructure and consumer-facing brand can make it an attractive partner.

articles.title: Hella Launches Commercial Vehicle Brake Pads
articles.author: Alex Crissey

paras.en: Hella Aftermarket is introducing brake pads for trucks, buses, and trailers, the company’s first offering in the commercial vehicle sector. The products are now available worldwide.

“We are starting with brake pads for trucks, buses, and trailers and will gradually expand the range,” says Dr. Marcel Wiedmann, head of the global aftermarket business at Forvia Hella. “Building on our established brake offering for passenger cars, we are now transferring our expertise to the commercial vehicle sector.”
Hella is launching an initial portfolio of 58 references, covering a range of applications and model variants, the company said.

The new program is designed for the high thermal and mechanical loads in heavy-duty applications. Each brake lining features matched friction materials to support braking performance, service life, and comfort in daily operation. Where necessary, linings are supplied with application-specific accessories.
All brake pads are tested and certified according to international safety and quality standards, including ECE R90.

articles.title: Dayco Expands Radiator Hose Line With 283 New Parts
articles.author: Jeff White

paras.en: Dayco is expanding its radiator hose line in response to key market indicators and growing demand. The company supplies engine products and drive systems to the automotive, industrial and aftermarket industries. The expansion will introduce 283 new hoses for complex vehicle applications.
Dayco Targets 90% Radiator Hose Coverage

The expansion will increase Dayco’s radiator hose coverage to 90% of vehicles in operation (VIO) by March 2027. That represents a 20% increase since 2025. Dayco will make 66 applications available in November and another 40 by year-end. The company will launch the remaining applications by the end of the first quarter of 2027.
The new part numbers include simple and branched hoses that meet stringent original equipment specifications for fit, form and function.

Industry trends helped drive Dayco’s hose line expansion. These include more vehicles approaching cooling system maintenance intervals. Today’s downsized turbocharged and high-performance engines also place greater demands on cooling systems and surrounding components.

“Between strong market drivers related to maintenance as well as an increase in demand, we prioritized an aggressive go-to-market strategy so we could introduce a significant number of new hose applications over the next several months,” said Jerry Reeves, head of product management for Dayco N.A. “This enables us to help our customers capture immediate market share while also enhancing our core value proposition.”
Dayco’s automotive hose line includes simple and branched designs for radiators, heaters, exhaust vents, fuel systems and other applications.

The company uses EPDM compounds and other materials to manufacture hoses for transferring fluids or gases. These hoses serve applications involving corrosive substances and high-pressure environments.
For more information on Dayco’s complete hose line, visit the company’s website.

articles.title: CRC Industries Showcasing Commitment to Skilled Trades at SEMA
articles.author: Mary DellaValle

paras.en: CRC Industries, a global provider of specialty chemicals for automotive maintenance and repair, announced it is expanding its investment in tomorrow’s automotive professionals at SEMA 2026 through initiatives designed to build awareness of skilled trades careers, create greater access to technical education, and support hands-on learning opportunities.

Through its Build for the Future initiative, created in partnership with TechForce Foundation, CRC is bringing each of these priorities to life. The program builds awareness of skilled trades careers through one-of-a-kind vehicle builds created alongside influential builders and automotive personalities; expands access to technical education through scholarship funding; and supports hands-on learning opportunities designed to help professionals build their skills.

At SEMA 2026, CRC said it will showcase the initiative’s latest build—a 1977 Chevrolet C10 Pro Street truck, which will cross the auction block at the Barrett-Jackson Scottsdale Auction in January 2027 to generate additional scholarship funding—alongside a new training trailer designed to support hands-on technical education.

“For generations, CRC has helped move the automotive industry forward through products and innovations professionals rely on every day. As industry leaders, we understand the importance of investing in the people who will shape its future,” said Len Mazzanti, CEO of CRC Industries. “Build for the Future brings our partners and the broader automotive community together to turn that commitment into meaningful opportunities for the next generation of skilled professionals.”
Building Awareness of Skilled Trade Careers

To generate scholarship funding, CRC partners with automotive personalities to create one-of-a-kind vehicles that generate excitement and visibility around careers in the skilled trades. Each build is showcased throughout the automotive community before heading to auction, where proceeds are turned into financial support for students pursuing technical education.

Built alongside longtime CRC collaborators Jeff Lutz of Lutz Race Cars and NHRA Top Fuel champion Clay Millican, the 1977 Chevrolet C10 brings together contributions from partners across the automotive industry. At its heart is an Edelbrock/Musi 555 carbureted big-block engine paired with an 8-71 supercharger, giving the classic C10 modern Pro Street performance.

Contributors to the project include Willie B (Two Guys Garage), Shaun Umscheid (“What No Way” Guy), Emily and Aaron Reeves (Flying Sparks Garage), and Mike Cotten (Faster with Newbern and Cotton), who served as the project’s Pro Street consultant.
The 1977 Chevrolet C10 Pro Street truck will be on display at CRC’s booth, No. 24677, in Central Hall.
Scholarships and Hands-On Technical Education

Through Build for the Future, CRC generates funding to award financial support to students pursuing technical school education, with each recipient receiving a minimum of $2,500. In 2026, CRC awarded 40 CRC Build for the Future scholarships of $2,500 each, totaling $100,000 across 17 automotive and industrial trades.

articles.title: Schaeffler Sets New Greenhouse Gas Reduction Targets
articles.author: Jeff White

paras.en: The Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi) has validated Schaeffler AG’s greenhouse gas emissions reduction targets. The organization confirmed that the targets meet its criteria and recommendations for near-term targets. The Schaeffler Group has further developed its sustainability strategy following its merger with Vitesco Technologies. The company achieved significant reductions through its previous strategy before the merger.
Schaeffler Targets Emissions Reductions by 2035
Schaeffler now aims to reduce absolute Scope 1 and 2 greenhouse gas emissions by 42% by 2035. The company will use 2025, the first fully consolidated year after the merger, as its base year.

The company also aims to reduce absolute Scope 3 emissions by 30% over the same period. These emissions include purchased goods and services, capital goods, fuel and energy activities, upstream transportation and distribution, operational waste and business travel.

“The validation of our climate targets by the Science Based Targets initiative marks an important milestone for Schaeffler on the path to climate neutrality. It means our climate targets are grounded in science, transparent and aligned with our responsibilities as a company. We recognize, however, that setting targets alone does not reduce emissions,” said Schaeffler CEO Klaus Rosenfeld. “The real work lies ahead. Further progress will be possible if we consistently align our actions with sustainability throughout our value chains. Following the acquisition of Vitesco, we are using 2025 as our new base year. We have a long-term perspective and are guided by our corporate values. For us, sustainability is both an obligation and an opportunity. Only by systematically integrating sustainability into our decisions and embedding it in our strategy can we lay the foundations for profitable growth and secure our long-term viability.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The Schaeffler Group supports the Paris Agreement and has set a goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2050. The SBTi has not validated this long-term goal, although it has validated the company’s two near-term targets.

Schaeffler aims to reduce Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions by 90% by 2050 compared with the 2025 base year. The company also plans to neutralize remaining emissions in accordance with applicable net-zero requirements.
The company’s Climate Transition Plan provides the framework for these efforts. Schaeffler established the plan in 2026 as part of its updated sustainability strategy.

Companies submit science-based climate targets to the Science Based Targets initiative or SBTi Services for validation. A formal review process determines whether the targets meet the SBTi’s criteria in effect at the time of submission.
The SBTi is a global organization that supports companies in setting science-based climate targets. Its work aligns with the Paris Agreement’s goal of limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius.
The organization develops standards, methods and guidelines for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. It also validates climate targets that companies submit.
The SBTi provides validation information on its website.

articles.title: How Simplification Can Create New Capacity for Growth
articles.author: Darcy Curran

paras.en: In the automotive aftermarket, growth is often associated with adding more: more products, more inventory, more suppliers and more resources. However, adding more doesn’t always lead to growth. In fact, adding more can introduce unnecessary complexity, making growth more difficult. The most successful businesses understand where they create the greatest value and have the discipline to direct resources toward those priorities.

No business can excel at everything. The most important strategic decision is often determining what not to do. Companies should first define what they want to be known for and how they can deliver distinctive value to customers. That requires discipline: investing in the right areas, focusing on the highest priorities, and stopping work that no longer advances the strategy.

Without this focus, complexity can surface quickly, and companies can wind up working too hard on the wrong things. The real cost isn’t limited to the time or dollars spent managing the complexity. More importantly, it includes potential growth opportunities missed because resources are not directed correctly.

Inventory management is one area where this can be seen. Healthy inventory turns consistently for suppliers and distributors, whereas chronically slow-moving inventory can signal that resources are not creating enough value for customers. Even inventory that isn’t moving still requires dollars to acquire, manage, store and move through the operation, and these costs can add up quickly, especially when the product isn’t generating meaningful sales.

As an important proactive action, suppliers and distributors should consistently review inventory investment and turns to help identify which products are creating value and where resources can be better focused to help drive growth.

The purchase price is easy to measure, and too often, businesses try to sell for the most and buy for the least. But greater value can come from understanding what partners need and where their challenges exist.

For distributors, there’s also value in building deeper relationships with a focused group of suppliers. During periods of supply disruption or elevated demand, manufacturers and other suppliers naturally prioritize their most important customers. These relationships create opportunities to support each other’s businesses better while establishing mutual trust and confidence.

In one supplier relationship, we learned a partner was looking to borrow money to fund an expansion. We had already planned to extend our contract, but by executing the agreement earlier, we gave our partner longer-term, predictable business, reducing their risk to their lender and allowing them to borrow at a lower rate. This early extension allowed both sides to get what they needed without simply negotiating over another percentage point on price.

The critical learning from this example is the importance of building relationships that are strategic rather than simply transactional. The most important question is: How can we change the way we do business to benefit both sides beyond the purchase order’s value? When distributors and suppliers understand each other’s businesses well enough to answer this question, the relationship can become stronger and create better economics for both sides.

Simplification also extends to how distributors serve their customers. By providing more flexibility in terms of how customers purchase and receive products, distributors can help customers manage their inventory more efficiently while maximizing their dollars and warehouse space.

Consider the difference between buying a case and a pallet: rather than putting significantly more cash into inventory up front, smaller quantities and more frequent replenishment can help align inventory more closely with demand.

That same principle can extend across the broader supplier relationship. When customers can access more of what they need in smaller quantities and combine categories into fewer shipments, they can simplify ordering and receiving, turn inventory faster and manage working capital and space more effectively.

Delivering that value also requires distributors to make smart decisions behind the scenes, specifically where distribution centers are located, how products move through them, and how far they travel to customers. All these decisions affect cost and reliability, specifically when distributing heavy, low-cost products. By adopting a more strategically positioned distribution network, distributors can reduce costs and improve service without increasing customer charges.

For Highline Warren, we start with a simple question: What do we want to be known for? We want customers to know that they can rely on us to deliver products on time and in full. Consistently delivering on those priorities builds credibility and can make a supplier more integral to the customer’s process, turning focus into a foundation for growth.

Understanding where a business creates value can also help identify its next growth opportunity. For suppliers and distributors, one of the easiest, fastest and most economical ways to grow is to sell existing products to existing customers. The relationship is already established, the supplier understands the customer, and the customer already knows the value the supplier provides. From there, a business should look at the broader market and consider how products or categories it already carries can help address another need.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: For example, a retailer may buy several product categories from one supplier while sourcing other products elsewhere, even though the same supplier already carries those products. The overlap creates an opportunity to grow by leveraging existing products and capabilities.

Growth frequently happens in concentric circles: first by strengthening existing relationships, then by expanding into adjacent opportunities that align with proven capabilities. Businesses that consistently deliver value earn the right to broaden those relationships over time.

Simplification isn’t simply about doing less. It is about being more deliberate and strategic about where a business puts its time, attention and resources, focusing on the areas that can drive meaningful growth.

Growth isn’t always about adding more; often, it comes from getting more from the products, capabilities and relationships a business has already established. Businesses disciplined enough to focus on this approach are better positioned to support customer needs, further strengthen relationships and create opportunities for mutual success.

articles.title: Universities should not be adopting AI to automate their own absurdities
articles.author: Akhil Bhardwaj

paras.en: Universities are at a critical point as students and faculty embrace the use of AI. Already, universities like Harvard are introducing courses that feature an AI avatar as an "instructor."

The promises AI offers higher education are familiar: an increase in efficiency as a consequence of less administration, more teaching coverage, better feedback and smarter assessment. But introducing artificial intelligence (AI) systems in an attempt to fix these problems is not the answer. If anything, AI systems will magnify and speed up the bureaucracy that is driving universities' decline.

In practice, the more likely outcome is darker: AI will not simply sweep away the bureaucratic machinery of universities; it will give that machinery a new regime of AI compliance — more policies, more forms, more trackers, more oversight roles and more work downloaded onto faculty who are already stretched thin.

The danger is not that AI will destroy universities but that universities will use AI to preserve the very processes that make them dysfunctional. If this happens, we might see faculty spending less time on research, less time on teaching, and more time on activities that do not directly contribute to the production of knowledge and education of students.

This is already evident in the existing assessment system in the U.K., but shades are creeping into systems elsewhere, providing a window into the future for U.S institutions. A single piece of student work may pass through a plagiarism-detection platform, a grading interface, a moderation spreadsheet for faculty to share feedback, a grade-transfer system, and an exam-board record. Each stage generates its own logins, deadlines, exception rules and audit trails. None of this is inherently malicious. Anonymous marking, moderation, appeals, accessibility and academic integrity are legitimate concerns. But when each concern is implemented as a separate system, the combined effect is administrative incoherence.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: In essence, faculty become the human interface between incompatible platforms, spending their time reconciling grades and chasing missing evidence rather than teaching. While this example pertains to U.K. universities, the trend to expand the administrative staff extends to North America. AI simply introduces a new opportunity to increase administration.

AI could, in principle, solve this. It could integrate systems, automate routine reporting, draft feedback, identify inconsistencies and remove duplicate data entry. Yet the institutional incentive is rarely to remove work; it is to make work visible. A university that automates a broken workflow does not necessarily simplify it. It may simply produce faster reports about the broken workflow, more sophisticated dashboards and more elaborate evidence of compliance. The bureaucratic impulse survives by changing its vocabulary: risk management, assurance, transparency, governance, responsible innovation.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: At least one possible outcome is that universities will create AI-use policies, require module-level AI statements, mandate disclosure forms, introduce approved-tool lists and establish review committees. Faculty will be asked to redesign assessments, monitor suspected misuse, document their decisions, complete training, and explain their approach to students. Much of this labor will be invisible. It will appear not as a new job title but as an additional expectation attached to teaching.

This creates a familiar pattern: responsibility without authority. Faculty are expected to make consequential judgments about academic integrity, fairness, privacy and assessment validity. But they do not control procurement, system design, institutional policy or disciplinary procedures. When something goes wrong, the academic is exposed; when the system works, the institution claims the credit.

That asymmetry is corrosive. It teaches committed staff that careful judgment is not valued as expertise but rather as a compliance risk to be managed, and the consequences will fall unevenly. Experienced faculty, after voicing their concern to no avail, may leave, retire early or disengage. Early-career academics, already precarious because they don't have tenure, will have the least power to resist. Students will receive less of the resource that matters most: sustained intellectual attention.

One possible outcome is that universities will encourage the development of faculty AI avatars and cut hours and employment. The institution will then justify hiring more — not fewer — compliance and "educational enhancement" staff to manage and maintain these AI avatars, negating the idea of efficiency and cost savings. In this scenario, bureaucracy will expand to manage the problems created by its own expansion while undercutting quality for the students who are paying high tuition fees. One might need to hire staff for oversight of these avatars, administrators and lawyers to manage licensing agreements, quality control staff in case things go wrong, and IT teams for integrating them into learning platforms and websites.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: - AI giants are one big mistake away from catastrophe. They could learn a lot from the nuclear industry.
- 'Autonomy always begins with something a human hands it': Who's responsible when an AI agent goes rogue?
- We're not about to awaken an evil digital god — AI is far more likely to end in a great disappointment

There is an alternative to the administrative tasks. AI should be governed by a simple institutional rule: no new compliance requirement without the removal of an equivalent existing burden. If a university requires assessment redesign to accommodate AI, or the introduction of new technology, it should provide protected time, technical support and a single integrated platform. If it expects faculty to manage AI use, it must give them clear institutional backing rather than leaving them to improvise. And critically, it should show how the technology makes work more efficient before rolling it out across the board.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: But the deeper issue is not technology but institutional purpose. A university exists — or should exist — to cultivate understanding, judgment and intellectual independence. If its systems consume faculty time, fragment the student experience, and reward documentation over learning, then AI becomes another instrument of managerial self-preservation. The question is not whether universities can adopt AI. It is whether they can resist using AI to automate their own absurdities.

If they cannot, the outcome will be an educational system that looks progressively sophisticated while becoming increasingly hollow — full of monitoring, low on trust; rich in measuring, poor in teaching; obsessed with compliance, indifferent to the people who make education possible; overly procedural sans intellectual life. It will become an audited theater of learning not worth students' time.

articles.title: First clear image of China's mysterious 'divine dragon' space plane revealed in US government report
articles.author: Harry Baker

paras.en: A new U.S. intelligence agency report has seemingly released the first clear photograph of China's mysterious "dragon" space plane in orbit around Earth. The surprise snap reveals that the top-secret vehicle is very similar to its American counterpart and provides new clues about its capabilities.

The image is widely believed to show China's secretive Shenlong, or "divine dragon," space plane, which has been in action for just over six years. During this time, the reusable winged spacecraft has repeatedly made headlines after deploying various unidentified objects in low Earth orbit (LEO). As a result, government officials, private companies and individual researchers have closely monitored the vehicle using tools such as ground-based radar.

Until now, the only direct images of the space plane have been blurry snaps of light reflecting off the uncrewed vehicle toward Earth's surface — offering no clear clues to its specific design, capabilities or intended purpose. China has also never publicly shared any photos of the vehicle or revealed any key information about its design.

On Monday (Oct. 26), the Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) released the latest version of its "Challenges to Security in Space" report, which assesses the various factors that pose a risk to American space assets. Deep within the 130-page document (on page 53), the authors included a previously unseen image of a "PCR [People's Republic of China] Spaceplane." The image's brief caption revealed that the photo had been taken in 2024 by a satellite belonging to the private space company Maxar Technologies, now known as Vantor.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The surprise inclusion of the photo was spotted and shared on the social platform X by journalist Andrew Jones, who specializes in China's space program and has previously shared crucial information about other ongoing missions.

Neither the caption nor the related section of the report made any mention of the photo being the first of its kind or explained why it was previously classified, raising questions about whether the authors realized its significance.

There is one small caveat. The report notes that China has two active space plane designs — Shenlong and Tengyun, meaning "cloud rider" — and the image's caption does not specify which design we are looking at, according to The Aviationist.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

However, there have been no confirmed launches of Tengyun to date. Existing photos of a potential prototype also hint that this vehicle's design looks markedly different from what we can see in the new photo. Therefore, most experts agree that the spacecraft in the image is most likely Shenlong.

Until now, all we really knew about Shenlong is that it operates similarly to NASA's iconic space shuttles: It gets launched into space by a rocket and circles Earth before eventually gliding down to the planet's surface, where it can then be refueled and relaunched into LEO.

It is not the world's only active space plane. The U.S. Space Force has its own, the X-37B, which has already completed seven orbital missions since its first launch in 2010 and is currently in LEO experimenting with quantum navigation. Based on the new photos, Shenlong shares many similarities with its American counterpart.

"The Chinese spaceplane has delta wings, payload bay doors, a dark heat shield, and a rear-mounted service module with power-generating solar arrays," technology news site ArsTechnica reported. "In other words, the design of the winged ship is, to a great degree, a copy of the X-37B spaceplane flown by the U.S. Space Force."

However, the two spacecraft are not exactly the same: "The overall arrangement resembles the American vehicle, although differences in wing geometry show that the two spacecraft are not externally identical," according to specialist news site Global Defense News.
It is still unclear how large Shenlong is. The X-37B is 29 feet (8.8 meters) long and has a wingspan of 15 feet (4.5 m), according to Popular Science.
The new image also indicates that Shenlong is most likely not a military asset, Global Defense News reported, noting that "the image does not establish a weapons role."
However, China likely has other space-based weapons, similar to the mysterious "in-orbit" American weapons recently confirmed by U.S. Air Force Secretary Troy E. Meink.

"China has developed and will continue to advance weapons for use against satellites in orbit to disrupt, damage, and destroy other nations' space capabilities," DIA representatives wrote in a separate section of the new report. "Beijing aims to become the preeminent leader in space," they added.

Since first launching into space on an initial two-day mission in September 2020, Shenlong has completed two feature-length missions: an eight-month stint in LEO between August 2022 and May 2023, and a nine-month spaceflight between December 2023 and September 2024. (The new image was taken during the latter mission).

The space plane is currently on its fourth mission, which launched Feb. 7 on board a Long March 2F rocket from China's Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center, Live Science's sister site Space.com previously reported. In total, Shenlong has racked up more than 800 days in orbit. However, it is unclear whether the same space plane was used on all four missions or if China has more than one space plane in use.
So far, Shelong has released at least nine unidentified payloads around Earth. These objects are most likely small satellites, known as cubesats, but their purpose remains unclear.
- Secretive Chinese probe snaps first photo of Earth's mysterious 'quasi-moon' — and it may pose a big problem
- China launches 'human artificial embryos' to space in bid to see whether reproduction is possible off-world
- New report warns that China could overtake the US as top nation in space — and it could happen 'in 5-10 years,' expert claims

The most recent object was deployed in June this year, although astronomer Jonathan McDowell, who specializes in tracking spacecraft in LEO, has since suggested that the spacecraft retrieved the object, potentially with a robotic arm, and rereleased it in late August.

The new report also mentions that the space plane "appeared to maneuver with a companion satellite" during its second mission in November 2022, coming within 330 feet (100 m) of the smaller spacecraft and potentially even capturing and re-releasing it.

This may support an existing theory that the main goal of Shenlong is to "conduct rendezvous and proximity operations" with other spacecraft, and that its payloads may be targets for it to practice flyby maneuvers in orbit.

Harry is a U.K.-based senior staff writer at Live Science. He studied marine biology at the University of Exeter before training to become a journalist. He covers a wide range of topics including space exploration, planetary science, space weather, climate change, animal behavior and paleontology. His recent work on the solar maximum won "best space submission" at the 2024 Aerospace Media Awards and was shortlisted in the "top scoop" category at the NCTJ Awards for Excellence in 2023. He also writes Live Science's weekly Earth from space series.

articles.title: Bronze Age sword discovered in an Italian lake is still sharp after 3,300 years
articles.author: Kristina Killgrove

paras.en: Archaeologists have recovered a well-preserved bronze sword from a volcanic lake in Italy. The 3,300-year-old weapon may have been deposited in the lake as an offering to a deity or for a high-status warrior who lived long before the rise of the Etruscans or the Romans.

The sword was found in Lake Mezzano, which is located in the crater of an ancient volcano roughly 60 miles (100 kilometers) northwest of Rome, according to a translated statement from the Superintendence of Archaeology, Fine Arts and Landscape for the Province of Viterbo and Southern Etruria. Dating to the Late Bronze Age (14th to 13th centuries B.C.), the sword has maintained its sharp edge. It is the third such sword found in Lake Mezzano in the past 50 years.

Bronze Age people erected pile dwellings or stilt houses in what is now Lake Mezzano, and archaeologists recovered parts of the submerged settlement during their recent investigations. According to the statement, researchers also found numerous intact vases, axes, arrowheads, daggers, spearheads, pins and a bronze razor.

The sword and the razor were found near each other, suggesting the two artifacts may have been linked to a person of high social status, such as an elite warrior. But the placement of the metal weapons in a lake may also be related to a wider Bronze Age ritual practice where hoards of jewelry and bent or ritually "killed" artifacts were tossed into bodies of water. This practice continued through the centuries into Etruscan times, when wells were ritually "closed" with artifacts and human sacrifices.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: During the 13th century B.C., people in central Italy engaged in trade networks that spanned the Mediterranean. "In this context, bronze weapons were not only instruments of combat, but also symbols of prestige, identity, and power," according to the statement.

The sword and other artifacts discovered in Lake Mezzano are giving archaeologists new information about the people who flourished in prehistoric Italy long before the Romans and Etruscans. Additional research is planned in the coming years, according to the statement.
Can you identify these historical objects of war? Test your smarts with our weapons of the world quiz!
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.
